content: Alendronate is prescribed to treat and prevent osteoporosis, a condition where bones become thin, weak, and prone to fractures, particularly in postmenopausal women. It is also used to manage osteoporosis in men and women taking corticosteroids, which can increase the risk of bone loss. Additionally, alendronate is used to treat Paget's disease of bone, a condition characterized by soft, weak, and deformed bones that may be painful or easily fractured. Alendronate belongs to a class of medications called bisphosphonates, which work by inhibiting bone breakdown and increasing bone density. Alendronate is available as a tablet or liquid solution to be taken orally. The liquid form is typically taken once a week on an empty stomach in the morning. The 5-mg and 10-mg tablets are usually taken daily on an empty stomach in the morning, while the 30-mg and 70-mg tablets are taken weekly under the same conditions. The 40-mg tablets are prescribed for daily use over six months to treat Paget's disease. It is crucial to follow the prescription instructions carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Taking alendronate incorrectly can reduce its effectiveness and may harm the esophagus or cause mouth sores. Alendronate must be taken immediately after getting out of bed in the morning, before consuming any food or drink. It should never be taken at bedtime or before rising for the day. Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass (6–8 ounces) of plain water. If taking the liquid form, follow it with at least 2 ounces of plain water. Avoid taking alendronate with any liquid other than plain water, such as tea, coffee, juice, milk, or sparkling water. Do not split, chew, crush, or suck on the tablets. After taking alendronate, refrain from eating, drinking, or taking other medications (including vitamins or antacids) for at least 30 minutes. Remain upright (sitting or standing) for at least 30 minutes after taking the medication and until you have eaten your first meal of the day. Alendronate helps manage osteoporosis and Paget's disease but does not cure these conditions. It may take three months or longer to observe an increase in bone density. The medication is effective only when taken regularly, so continue using it even if you feel well. Do not stop taking alendronate without consulting your doctor. Before starting alendronate, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to it, any other medications, or any of its ingredients. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Mention specific medications such as aspirin, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), cancer chemotherapy, or oral steroids (e.g., dexamethasone, prednisone). Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. If you are unable to sit or stand upright for at least 30 minutes, or if you have a history of low blood calcium levels or esophageal problems, inform your doctor, as alendronate may not be suitable for you. Additionally, disclose any history of radiation therapy, anemia, swallowing difficulties, heartburn, ulcers, stomach issues, cancer, infections (especially in the mouth), dental or gum problems, blood clotting disorders, or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning to become pregnant, inform your doctor, as alendronate can remain in the body for years after discontinuation. Notify your doctor immediately if you become pregnant during or after treatment. Alendronate may cause serious jaw problems, particularly if you undergo dental surgery or treatment while taking the medication. Have a dentist examine your teeth and perform any necessary treatments before starting alendronate. Maintain good oral hygiene and consult your doctor before undergoing any dental procedures while on this medication. Improper use of alendronate can cause severe damage to the lining of the mouth, esophagus, or stomach. If you experience new or worsening heartburn, difficulty swallowing, pain when swallowing, or chest pain, stop taking alendronate and contact your doctor immediately. To prevent osteoporosis, your doctor may recommend lifestyle changes such as avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol consumption, and engaging in regular weight-bearing exercises. Additionally, consume foods and drinks rich in calcium and vitamin D. If dietary intake is insufficient, your doctor may prescribe or recommend supplements. If you miss a daily dose of alendronate, skip the missed dose and take the next dose the following morning as usual. For weekly doses, take the missed dose the morning after you remember, then resume your regular weekly schedule. Never take more than one dose in a single day or double up on doses to compensate for a missed one. Alendronate may cause side effects. Common minor side effects include nausea, stomach pain, constipation, diarrhea, gas, bloating, changes in taste, bone or muscle pain, headache, dizziness, and flu-like symptoms. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention. These include new or worsening heartburn, difficulty swallowing, pain when swallowing, chest pain, bloody vomit or vomit resembling coffee grounds, black or bloody stools, fever, skin blisters or peeling, rash (worsened by sunlight), itching, hives, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, hoarseness, painful or swollen gums, loose teeth, jaw numbness or heaviness, poor jaw healing, and eye pain. Contact your doctor if you experience any unusual problems while taking alendronate. Store alendronate in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom or freeze the liquid form. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. In case of overdose, give the person a full glass of milk and contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the person collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Do not allow the person to lie down or induce vomiting. Symptoms of overdose include heartburn, nausea, stomach pain, bloody vomit, difficulty swallowing, and black or bloody stools. Keep all medical and laboratory appointments, as your doctor may order tests to monitor your response to alendronate. Do not share this medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refilling your prescription.
